passage:
Sunday. At lunch, Chinmay's father put down his glass. "Ankita's coaching fee is due, and the roof needs mending before the rains. You're the elder son, Chinmay. You'll manage." His mother nodded. Chinmay, back from a night shift, nodded too and reached for the rice.
Wednesday. He fell asleep on the bus and missed his stop by three stations. At his desk, he stared at the form for the exam he had wanted to take since March. The deadline was that Friday. He closed the tab.
Saturday. His younger sister Ankita found him on the terrace. "Bhaiya, you look so tired." "I'm fine." "You always say that." She sat beside him. Nobody had said it in months. He felt his throat tighten. "I'm not fine," he said, finally. "Not always."

qa.q: Which family member's coaching fee was due?
What was Chinmay feeling when he closed the tab for the exam form?
qa.a: Chinmay felt worn out and quietly disappointed, giving up something he had wanted. His family duties left no room for it.

qa.q: What turning point on Saturday gave Chinmay a way forward?
qa.a: Ankita told him he looked tired and stayed beside him, and Chinmay finally said he was not always fine. Saying it aloud was the first step to being seen.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's father see his elder son's role?
qa.a: The father likely believes he is honouring a sincere duty and that Chinmay can manage. He may not have noticed the cost, since Chinmay nodded and said nothing.

grounding: An eldest son expected to sacrifice for everyone feels unseen when tired; the duty is sincere but costs more than one person can pay.

passage:
Noor, you said your family expects you to carry everything as the eldest daughter. Let me tell you about mine. I'm Akash, and at twenty-five I was the eldest son. My salary paid for my brother's fees, my mother's medical visits and the loan on the shop. Nobody was unkind. My father said thank you every month. But nobody asked me if I was tired.
One evening my Nani stopped me at the door. "Eat," she said, and put a bowl in my hands. "You look thinner than the rice." I sat down and cried, right there.
Next morning I told my mother, "I can pay for this half, but not all." She was quiet, then said, "I did not know you were so tired." It didn't fix everything, but it was the first time we talked about it.

qa.q: What did Akash's salary pay for at twenty-five?
qa.a: It paid for a brother's fees, a mother's medical visits and the loan on the shop.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Nani put a bowl of food into Akash's hands?
qa.a: Akash felt exhausted and unseen, and being noticed at last released it in tears.

qa.q: What choice did Akash make the next morning?
qa.a: Akash told the mother that half could be paid but not all. That started an honest conversation about the tiredness.

qa.q: How did Akash's mother seem to feel on hearing that Akash was tired?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and perhaps sorry, since she said she had not known. Her quiet suggests she had not seen the cost of her son's giving.

grounding: An eldest child expected to sacrifice for everyone feels unseen until someone notices how tired he is; the duty was sincere but costly.
